captions.text: In 1872, an artist painted a wild canyon in Yellowstone.
That year, Yellowstone became the world's first national park.
Bison had almost disappeared. Inside the park, they were safe.
A whole park? Just for nature?
Far away in Florida, a spoonbill flies over the Everglades.
Zoom out. It lives in a river of grass, up to 60 miles wide.
So why do people work so hard to protect wild places like this?

words: Land the government sets aside to keep wild and safe from harmful building.
The variety of different plants and animals living together in one place.
The natural home where a plant or animal finds food, water, and shelter.

parts.title: What Is Protected Land?
parts.html:
Some land in the United States is set aside by law. Nobody can build houses, factories, or farms there. These are protected lands.

National parks are one kind of protected land. People can visit and explore them, but the plants, animals, and water inside are kept safe from the kind of damage people can cause.

parts.title: Why Biodiversity Matters
parts.html:
A healthy ecosystem has many different kinds of living things. That variety is called biodiversity. Each species plays a role. Bees pollinate flowers. Owls eat mice. Decomposers break down dead leaves.

When one species disappears, others can be affected. A place with many kinds of living things is steadier and harder to break.

parts.title: How Conservation Works
parts.html: Rangers and scientists work inside national parks. They count animals, pull out invasive plants, and reduce pollution. About half of the original Everglades was drained for farms and cities. Today much of what's left is protected, and scientists are slowly helping it recover.

compare.title: Which place can lose a species and stay healthy?
compare.look: Two real places, each on a lit specimen tray. Specimen A is a Florida wetland where many kinds of birds feed together. Specimen B is a giant farm field where one kind of plant grows. A food web is a map of who eats whom. Under the trays are two model tests: scissors to snip one species out of the web, and a fence to keep people out.

trays.alt: Pink spoonbills, white egrets, and wood storks feeding together in shallow water
trays.label: Specimen A

trays.alt: Long, straight rows of green sugarcane fields stretching to the horizon, seen from an airplane
trays.label: Specimen B

ask.q: Which place has many kinds of living things?
ask.ok: Yes. Specimen A has spoonbills, egrets, storks, fish, and more.
ask.miss: Look closely. Which one has lots of different birds?

ask.q: Which place has mostly one kind of plant?
ask.ok: Yes. Specimen B is row after row of sugarcane.
ask.miss: Look again. Which one has the same plant everywhere?

compare.testDo: Put the scissors under one tray and the fence under the other: drag them, or tap one, then a tray. Press Run the test. Then swap.
compare.disclaimer: This is a model. Real food webs have thousands of links.

Asnip.text: One bird is snipped out. The web wobbles, but other animals still have food. The web holds.

Afence.text: The fence keeps people out. The busy web stays busy.

Bsnip.text: One species is snipped out. With so few kinds, nothing fills its place, and the web falls apart.

Bfence.text: A fence can't add missing species. The thin web stays thin.

compare.frame: This place has ___, so when one species is lost, its web ___.
compare.claimMid: so when one species is lost, its web

curator.A: High biodiversity → a strong web. When one species is lost, others fill in.
curator.B: Low biodiversity → a weak web. Losing one species can break it.

after.kicker: 🎬 Behind the scenes · Only in South Florida
after.alt: An American crocodile with a long, narrow snout resting on a gray rock by the water
after.html: South Florida is the only place in the world where American alligators and American crocodiles live side by side in the wild. Everglades and Biscayne National Parks protect both. Crocodiles like salty water near the coast; alligators like fresh water.

predict.q: Is a protected ocean park home to just a few kinds of animals, or many?
predict.mine: Your prediction: {p}. Let's dive down and find out.
predict.confirm: You predicted many kinds. The evidence agrees: different animals live at every depth, from the surface to the deep reef.

wall.skyAlt: A six-sided brick fort on a small island ringed by bright blue-green water
wall.skyCap: Fort Jefferson · Dry Tortugas National Park, Florida
wall.locked: Brush the stop above first. We dive down one stop at a time.
wall.first: Brush the glowing top stop. Drag across it (or tap it again and again).
wall.endText: Look at the line. Every depth has its own animals: snorkelers at the top, turtles in the seagrass, fish on the coral, and giant groupers in the deep. Protect the park, and you protect them all.
wall.rule: More kinds, more connections. A protected ocean park keeps many habitats safe at once, from shallow seagrass to deep reefs. Fishing limits and no-anchor zones help the reef keep its biodiversity.

mix.q: A friend says, "Losing one kind of fish from the reef doesn't matter." Is that right?

options.t: Right. There are lots of other fish.
options.miss: Think about the Web Test. What happened when one species was snipped from a web?

options.t: No. Every species has a job, and losing one can affect others.
options.ok: Yes! Parrotfish keep algae off the coral, groupers eat other fish, and turtles trim the seagrass. Each one matters.

wow.title: The bison came back
wow.alt: A herd of bison grazing in a green valley with fog drifting over the dark forest behind them
wow.caption: A bison herd on a foggy morning · Lamar Valley, Yellowstone National Park
wow.html:
Millions of bison once roamed North America. Hunters killed so many that by the early 1900s, only about two dozen wild bison were left in Yellowstone.

The park protected them and brought in more. Today thousands of bison roam Yellowstone. They're the only place in the United States where wild bison have lived since prehistoric times.
wow.insetCap: Bison grazing in Lamar Valley, Yellowstone.

keyIdea: Protecting land protects the whole ecosystem: the soil, water, plants, and animals that all depend on each other. Places with high biodiversity are steadier, so when people protect wild land, they help many species at once. Human choices can harm wild habitats, and human choices can protect them.
